body.statement: Let \(\mathscr P\) be a finite family of real polynomials in two real variables and let \(B\) be a closed rectangle. There is a finite semialgebraic partition \(\mathscr C\) of \(B\) such that every polynomial in \(\mathscr P\) has constant sign on each member, every member is relatively connected, and for every \(C,D\in\mathscr C\) either \(D\subseteq\overline C^{B}\) or \(D\cap\overline C^{B}=\varnothing\). Consequently, for any two unions \(A_0,A_1\) of members of \(\mathscr C\), the set \(\overline{A_0}^{B}\cap\overline{A_1}^{B}\) is a union of members of a finite refinement, and a retained member is contained in that intersection if and only if every relative neighborhood of each of its points meets both \(A_0\) and \(A_1\). If the coefficients and rectangle vertices are rational, the partition, all frontier incidences, and all nonemptiness and sign claims admit exact finite certificates based on rational univariate root isolation and polynomial remainder signs.
body.proof_tex:
We give a finite construction. First adjoin the four affine facet polynomials of \(B\) to \(\mathscr P\). Regard each member of the enlarged family as a polynomial in the second coordinate. Form a finite projection list in the first coordinate consisting of all nonzero coefficients, square-free parts, discriminants, and principal subresultant coefficients of pairs drawn from \(\mathscr P\) and their derivatives with respect to the second coordinate. Close this operation once more under greatest-common-divisor remainder coefficients. The list is finite because the original degrees and cardinality are finite, and its entries have rational coefficients whenever the input coefficients do.

Isolate all real roots of the projection list in the first-coordinate interval. This produces finitely many point cells and open interval cells. Over an open interval cell, the signs of all projection polynomials are constant. The leading-coefficient signs fix degrees; the subresultant signs fix the degrees of all relevant greatest common divisors and hence the multiplicities and coincidences of roots. After splitting by these fixed square-free factors, every real root is simple in its factor. The implicit-function argument is elementary here: if \(p(a,b)=0\) and \(\partial p/\partial y(a,b)\neq0\), continuity and the intermediate-value theorem give a unique root near \(b\), and the difference quotient equation shows that this root varies continuously with \(a\). Because roots cannot meet without the corresponding discriminant or resultant vanishing, the finitely many root graphs retain their order throughout the interval cell. Their graphs and the open sectors between consecutive graphs therefore partition the vertical cylinder into relatively connected semialgebraic cells on which every polynomial in \(\mathscr P\) has constant sign. Over a point cell, ordinary univariate root isolation in the second coordinate gives the analogous finite collection of point and interval cells.

Refine at every endpoint limit of every root graph and at every coincidence recorded by a zero resultant. A section can approach only a root of the specialized endpoint polynomial: if \((a_n,b_n)\) lies on the section and converges to \((a,b)\), polynomial continuity gives \(p(a,b)=0\). Conversely, the isolating intervals and the fixed root ordering identify exactly which sections and sectors approach each endpoint cell. Splitting the endpoint cells at those finitely many limiting roots makes the following incidence alternative hold for each pair of cells:
\[
 D\subseteq\overline C^{B}
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 D\cap\overline C^{B}=\varnothing.
\]
There are finitely many cells and pairs, so this refinement terminates. It preserves sign invariance and relative connectedness.

For completeness, suppose now that all input coefficients and rectangle vertices are rational. For a square-free rational univariate polynomial \(p\), put \(p_0=p\), \(p_1=p'\), and recursively let \(p_{i+1}\) be the negative Euclidean remainder of \(p_{i-1}\) on division by \(p_i\). Degrees strictly decrease, so the sequence is finite. At a zero of an intermediate \(p_i\), the recurrence gives \(p_{i-1}=-p_{i+1}\), and the number of sign variations is unchanged when that point is crossed. At a root of \(p_0\), square-freeness gives \(p_1\neq0\), and the defining derivative sign shows that the variation count drops by one from left to right. It follows, by partitioning an interval at all zeros of the sequence, that the difference of endpoint variation counts equals the number of roots of \(p\) in the interval. Repeated rational bisection therefore yields disjoint rational isolating intervals, one per root. Signs of another polynomial at an isolated algebraic root are determined by its signed remainder sequence with \(p\), with a zero sign detected by their greatest common divisor. Thus the cells, signs, root order, and frontier incidences have finite rational certificates.

Let \(A_0,A_1\) be unions of cells. By the incidence alternative, a cell \(D\) is contained in \(\overline{A_i}^{B}\) exactly when it lies in the closure of at least one cell contained in \(A_i\). Hence each closure, and their intersection, is a union of cells after the displayed finite refinement. Finally, a point belongs to \(\overline{A_i}^{B}\) exactly when every relative \(B\)-neighborhood meets \(A_i\), by the definition of closure. Applying this equivalence to \(i=0,1\) proves the pointwise neighborhood criterion and completes the construction.
